Discussion It is challenging to formulate effective treatment options for IBS since the symptom likely represents a variety of medical conditions ( 36 ). One of the main symptoms of IBS and the primary explanation for why patients seek medical attention is abdominal pain related to bowel movements ( 37 , 38 ). Although there are a number of well-established management solutions, their availability varies, and their use is not always ideal ( 39 ). For vulnerable individuals experiencing extreme pain, it is necessary to avoid iatrogenesis and uncontrolled, inadequately supported methods. Although there is a promising pipeline of new preclinical and early clinical targets and management strategies, there are still a lot of unanswered questions; thus, pain in IBS continues to be a focus for quality improvement and research ( 40 ). Our systematic analysis of GLP-1 agonist’s impact on IBS-related pain and symptoms suggests a promising landscape for its use beyond standard metabolic applications. GLP-1 receptor agonists’ multifaceted therapeutic properties extend their benefits to a wide range of pain disorders, including inflammatory, visceral, and neuropathic pain ( 41 , 42 ). This meta-analysis demonstrated that ROSE-010 significantly lowers pain intensity in patients with IBS compared to a placebo. The odds ratios for the 100 µg and 300 µg doses show a significant positive effect. The low variability across trials increases the reliability of these findings. The meta-analysis supports ROSE-010’s effectiveness in treating IBS symptoms. Previous studies provided comparative results and evidence that ROSE-010 is effective in controlling pain and improving gastrointestinal motility in IBS patients. Hellström et al. (2009) conducted a placebo-controlled experiment to assess the effectiveness of ROSE-010 in relieving pain in all IBS subtypes. The trial included two doses. The results showed that at one hour post-treatment, the ROSE-010 groups had twice as many pain alleviation responders as the placebo group. The study additionally showed that ROSE-010 was most helpful at relieving pain in IBS-C and IBS-M ( 24 ). Touny et al. (2022) conducted a cross-analysis to assess the pain alleviation and intensity responses to ROSE-010 in IBS patients. The trial involved 166 subjects and concluded that ROSE-010 provided dosage- and time-dependent pain alleviation, with the highest relief obtained at the 300 µg dose. Females reported more pain reduction than males, and the drug was more beneficial for IBS-C and IBS-M ( 12 ). Halloum et al. (2024) conducted a systematic review to assess the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as ROSE-010, for headache and pain concerns. The review stated that GLP-1 receptor agonists have analgesic properties by modifying pain hypersensitivity in animal models of inflammation and neuropathic pain. The review also found that GLP-1 receptor agonists diminish visceral hypersensitivity and alleviate symptoms in IBS patients ( 43 ). GLP-1 agonists, such as ROSE-010, relieve pain in IBS patients by altering gut motility ( 43 ), lowering inflammation ( 44 ), modulating neurotransmitters ( 45 ), reducing visceral hypersensitivity ( 46 ), and interacting with the gut microbiota ( 47 ). These pathways help to explain GLP-1 agonists’ pain-relieving benefits in IBS patients. They can help reduce visceral hypersensitivity, a frequent symptom in IBS ( 48 , 49 ). Following meal consumption, the metabolic endocrine cascade begins with gastric emptying. Insulin secretion is stimulated, glucagon and gastric acid secretion are inhibited, and GI transit and motility are decreased by incretin hormones, especially GLP-1, which is released postprandially from L-cells lining the gut in response to food ingestion ( 50 – 52 ). Furthermore, both in vitro and in vivo , GLP-1 has been frequently demonstrated to reduce GI muscle activity via nerve-mediated mechanisms reliant on nitric oxide ( 13 , 53 ). In addition to being expressed in peripheral tissues, the GLP-1 receptor is also expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) and is limited to neurons in the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and the ventrolateral medulla in the brainstem and hypothalamus ( 54 , 55 ). Biologically active GLP-1 has a high affinity for this receptor ( 56 , 57 ). Additionally, the GLP-1 receptors has been identified in the GI tract’s myenteric and submucosal neural plexuses ( 55 ). GLP-1 inhibited the migrating motor complex (MMC) and decreased motility in the antro-duodeno-jejunal region in both healthy subjects and IBS patients ( 22 ). Constipation-predominant IBS was linked to lower mucosal expression of GLP-1R and blood GLP-1 concentrations ( 28 ). It is believed that reduced concentrations of GLP-1 would result in loss of the pro-kinetic actions of GLP-1 in the colon [Citation26], causing constipation and abdominal discomfort, was further supported by the correlation between this and the intensity of abdominal pain ( 12 ). A rat model of visceral pain sensitivity also showed a reduction in circulating amounts of bioactive GLP-1 ( 58 ). GLP-1 and ROSE-010 suppress postprandial GI motility, most likely via GLP-1R at myenteric neurons, necessitating functioning cAMP and nitrergic signaling ( 13 ). According to the current study’s findings, ROSE-010 is linked to a greater incidence of headaches, nausea, and vomiting than placebo. These adverse effects are probably caused by the drugs themselves rather than by extraneous factors, as indicated by the results’ consistency across several studies and low degree of heterogeneity. It seems that ROSE-010 has demonstrated encouraging outcomes in treating acute pain in people with IBS, as compared to earlier research. But of particular concern is the increase in headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Adverse effects have been documented in prior studies ( 12 , 21 , 24 ), suggesting that although ROSE-010 is useful in treating pain, its tolerance profile should be carefully evaluated. Several medications have been approved for the management of IBS, each targeting a particular mechanism and use for a specific disease subtype. In contrast to pure μ-opioid agonists, eluxadoline, a little-absorbed combined μ- and κ-opioid receptor agonist and δ-opioid receptor antagonist, was developed to decrease constipation and boost analgesic effectiveness ( 59 , 60 ). The FDA has authorized 100 mg of eluxadoline twice daily for the treatment of IBS-D. Patients with mild to severe hepatic impairment, those using concurrent OATP1B1 inhibitors, or those who can’t tolerate the 100 mg dosage are advised to use eluxadoline 75 mg twice daily ( 61 ). Constipation (8%), nausea (7%), and stomach pain (7%), among individuals receiving eluxadoline, were the most frequent side effects ( 61 ). Gram-positive and gram-negative anaerobic and aerobic bacteria are both susceptible to the wide-ranging effects of the nonabsorbable oral antibiotic rifaximin ( 62 ). The FDA has approved a dose of 550 mg three times a day for 14 days to treat IBS-D. Using the same dosing schedule, patients can receive treatment up to twice if their symptoms return ( 63 ). Nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infections, upper respiratory infections, and nausea were the most frequent side effects ( 64 ). The mechanism of action of the selective 5-HT3 antagonist alosetron is thought to be both centrally and peripherally mediated ( 65 ). The FDA first authorized Alosetron in 2000 to treat IBS-D in women. However, it was voluntarily discontinued because of severe side effects, including ischemic colitis and severe constipation problems ( 66 ). Alosetron’s reintroduction was authorized by the FDA in 2002, but it was limited to treating women with severe IBS-D as part of a risk-management program ( 67 ). Half mg twice daily is the first suggested starting dose. Patients who have constipation should stop taking the drug until their symptoms relieve. They can resume taking 0.5 mg once daily, but alosetron should be stopped if constipation returns at a lower dosage. After four weeks, the dose can be raised to 1 mg twice a day if symptoms are still uncontrollable. Alosetron should be stopped after 4 weeks if symptoms still exist, even if the dosage is increased to 1 mg twice a day ( 61 ). In clinical practice, antispasmodics are frequently used for alleviating IBS-related abdominal pain. Despite being a pharmacologically varied class, antispasmodics are believed to alleviate the symptoms of IBS by lowering visceral hypersensitivity and smooth muscle contraction ( 68 ). The only antispasmodics that are accessible in the US are peppermint oil, hyoscine, and dicyclomine. Compared to the previously discussed side effects of approved IBS medications, ROSE-010 is typically well tolerated; however, adverse events (AEs) can occur. The expected medication effects, which include nausea, vomiting, and headache, are rarely severe ( 21 , 24 ). The current study has certain limitations. The meta-analysis, based on a limited sample size of five studies, may impact the statistical power and generalizability of the findings. The restricted number of studies also raises issues about the representativeness of the findings. Future research should prioritize larger, well-designed studies to increase statistical power, reliability, and generalizability. Subgroup analysis according to IBS subtypes (e.g., IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M, and IBS-U) would have offered significant insight on how the intervention differed in its effects on these various patient groups. However, such subgroup analyses were not possible because of the small number of studies. Given that there are several subtypes of IBS and that the condition’s etiology and symptom profiles vary, this is another limitation of the study. Furthermore, the study’s absence of comparisons to other medications may make it difficult to implement ROSE-010 in the current therapy landscape. As a result, more clinical trials are needed to better understand ROSE-010’s potential for IBS management. The suggested clinical trial pipeline involves longitudinal investigations, randomized controlled trials, post-marketing surveillance, as well as health economic analysis. It attempts to address the knowledge gaps and give a comprehensive understanding of the treatment’s long-term effects, resulting in better clinical decisions and patient outcomes. Conclusion The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist ROSE-010 has been shown in studies to be beneficial in lowering the severity of pain in individuals with IBS. The drug’s reliability is demonstrated by the findings, which are consistent throughout several trials. However, the higher frequency of headaches, nausea, and vomiting at the 100 µg dosage emphasizes the necessity of close monitoring. The study also highlights the value of individualized treatment plans that modify therapy according to the unique needs of each patient. The impact on various IBS subtypes, methods of action, and long-term effects require more investigation. Clinical recommendations and guidelines for the use of ROSE-010 in the treatment of IBS may be influenced by the findings of this study. To maximize outcomes, healthcare professionals must balance the advantages against the possibility of side effects and take individualized treatment modalities into account. documents.title: Effects of Infant Formula Supplemented With Prebiotics on the Gut Microbiome, Gut Environment, Growth Parameters, and Safety and Tolerance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
documents.abstract:
CONTEXT: Prebiotics are often added to infant formulas to mimic the benefits of oligosaccharides found in human milk.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of prebiotic-supplemented cow's milk-based formula on the gut microbiota, gut environment, growth parameters, and safety and tolerance in infants ≤6 months old, compared with a standard formula or human milk comparator.
DATA SOURCES: Searches were performed in the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses databases. Articles were included that reported on randomized controlled trials, were published from inception until April 2024, and met prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria.
DATA EXTRACTION: Outcomes included gut microbiota (eg, diversity; taxa at phylum, family, genus and species levels), gut environment (eg, pH, secretory immunoglobulin A, fecal calprotectin, fecal metabolites), growth parameters (eg, z scores), and safety and tolerance. Fixed or random effects models were used and mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were calculated to assess pooled effects. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration Tool (RoB 2).
DATA ANALYSIS: A total of 30 articles met inclusion criteria, with 5290 infants included. Whereas effects on Lactobacillus were inconsistent, prebiotic formula supplementation increased Bifidobacterium counts (k = 7 [MD: 0.49; 95% CI, 0.27-0.71]; I2 = 13%; P < .00001) and decreased fecal pH (k = 7 [MD: -0.39; 95% CI, -0.57 to -0.20]; I2 = 0%; P < .0001) compared with standard formula. Prebiotic formula supplementation increased total bacteria compared with human milk (MD: 0.41 [95% CI, 0.17-0.65]; I2 = 8%; P = .0006). In terms of growth parameters, weight-for-age z scores favored the prebiotic formula group compared with the human milk group (k = 2 [MD: 0.23; 95% CI, 0.04-0.42]; I2 = 7%; P = .02).
CONCLUSIONS: Prebiotic supplementation in infant formula can positively alter the gut microbiota, particularly Bifidobacterium, without negative impacts on growth. Standardized, high-quality research is needed to confirm the study findings and inform guidelines for prebiotic use in infant nutrition.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration no. CRD42021253589.
documents.conclusions:
Prebiotic supplementation in infant formula can positively alter the gut microbiota, particularly Bifidobacterium, without negative impacts on growth. Standardized, high-quality research is needed to confirm the study findings and inform guidelines for prebiotic use in infant nutrition.

For commercial re-use, please contact journals.permissions@oup.com Abstract Context Prebiotics are often added to infant formulas to mimic the benefits of oligosaccharides found in human milk. Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of prebiotic-supplemented cow’s milk–based formula on the gut microbiota, gut environment, growth parameters, and safety and tolerance in infants ≤6 months old, compared with a standard formula or human milk comparator. Data Sources Searches were performed in the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses databases. Articles were included that reported on randomized controlled trials, were published from inception until April 2024, and met prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data Extraction Outcomes included gut microbiota (eg, diversity; taxa at phylum, family, genus and species levels), gut environment (eg, pH, secretory immunoglobulin A, fecal calprotectin, fecal metabolites), growth parameters (eg, z scores), and safety and tolerance. Fixed or random effects models were used and mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were calculated to assess pooled effects. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration Tool (RoB 2). Data Analysis A total of 30 articles met inclusion criteria, with 5290 infants included. Whereas effects on Lactobacillus were inconsistent, prebiotic formula supplementation increased Bifidobacterium counts ( k = 7 [MD: 0.49; 95% CI, 0.27-0.71]; I 2 = 13%; P < .00001) and decreased fecal pH ( k = 7 [MD: –0.39; 95% CI, –0.57 to –0.20]; I 2 = 0%; P < .0001) compared with standard formula. Prebiotic formula supplementation increased total bacteria compared with human milk (MD: 0.41 [95% CI, 0.17-0.65]; I 2 = 8%; P = .0006). In terms of growth parameters, weight-for-age z scores favored the prebiotic formula group compared with the human milk group ( k = 2 [MD: 0.23; 95% CI, 0.04-0.42]; I 2 = 7%; P = .02). Conclusions Prebiotic supplementation in infant formula can positively alter the gut microbiota, particularly Bifidobacterium , without negative impacts on growth. Standardized, high-quality research is needed to confirm the study findings and inform guidelines for prebiotic use in infant nutrition. Systematic Review Registration PROSPERO registration no. INTRODUCTION The human gut harbors a complex microbial ecosystem. The gastrointestinal tract of a fetus in utero is generally thought to be sterile. 1 As newborns enter the extrauterine environment, they encounter their first contact with microbes, either from the vagina or birthing environment. 2 After the first inoculation, the infant gut undergoes substantial reorganization. During the first 3 months of life, the infant gut microbiota is predominantly composed of Bifidobacterium . 3 It then transitions from an initial low microbial diversity and complexity to a mature, adult-like state, characterized by higher alpha diversity, around 3 years of age. 3 Subsequent development of the intestinal microbiota plays an important role in normal growth, maturation of the immune system, and protection against infections. 4 , 5 The first few years of life, therefore, are critical periods for intervention in shaping the microbiota. Several parameters influence gut microbial colonization, including delivery mode, duration of gestation, country of birth, antibiotic use, and feeding modality. 6 Human milk feeding is the recommended nutritional source for infants in the first 6 months of life. 7 In the absence of a mother’s own human milk, infant formula derived from cow’s milk becomes the available alternative. Prebiotics increasingly have been added to infant formula to mimic the fermentable component of human milk, namely the human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). According to the recent consensus statement of the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics, a prebiotic is defined as “a substrate that is selectively used by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit.” 8 Prebiotics are nondigestible food ingredients that pass into the lower gastrointestinal tract unchanged. In the colon, they may be selectively metabolized by mutualistic microorganisms, such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus . Therefore, prebiotics may directly influence the composition and activity of the gut microbiome and may contribute to improved host health. Prebiotic oligosaccharides are an example of a dietary fiber that cannot be hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes, and they enter the colon intact before undergoing bacterial fermentation. 9 More than 130 oligosaccharides have been identified in human milk, constituting the third most abundant component of human milk. 10 In infant formula, a specific mixture of galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS) and fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS) is commonly added to stimulate the growth of Bifidobacterium 11–13 and Lactobacillus, 14 suppress pathogens, 15 and generate short-chain fatty acids, 16 , 17 similar to the oligosaccharides found naturally in human milk. The prebiotics inulin and oligofructose (OF) have shape gut-associated lymphoid tissue parameters and functions in animal models, such as the concentration of secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA). 18 A previous systematic review conducted in 2011 by the European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) concluded that prebiotic supplementation of infant formula has no adverse effects on infant growth. 19 However, given heterogeneity in the data, the committee recommended more studies be conducted before making recommendations on the routine use of prebiotic-supplemented formula. A recent systematic review examined the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on infant gut microbiota. 20 However, that review differs from ours in several ways. First, the review selected trials from 2010-2021 that did not include formula supplemented purely with prebiotics. Second, the review only examined the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on genus-level bacteria (not phylum, family, or species), and did not examine growth parameters as a health outcome. Third, the review only examined standard formula (not human milk) as a comparator. Fourth, the review did not include a meta-analysis. Finally, the population studied included infants recruited only within the first 2 months of life. Our aim was to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize the evidence (up to 2024) on the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula compared with standard formula or human milk on the (1) composition of the gut microbiota (phylum, family, genus, and species levels), (2) gut environment, (3) growth parameters (infant anthropometrics), and (4) safety and tolerance profile in infants 6 months of age or younger. METHODS Study Design This systematic review and meta-analysis were registered on the PROSPERO database (CRD42021253589) and followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA) reporting guidelines. 21 It was completed between June 2021 and June 2024. The infant gut microbiome was operationalized as alpha and beta diversities, taxa, and function. The infant gut environment was operationalized as gut integrity, inflammation, and metabolites, including pH, sIgA, fecal calprotectin, and fecal short- and branched-chain fatty acids. Infant growth parameters were operationalized as weight, weight gain, length, length gain, head circumference, weight-for-age z scores, body mass index–for-age z scores, skinfold thickness, fat mass or percent fat mass, and fat-free mass or percent fat-free mass. Adverse events refer to safety and tolerance such as digestive symptoms and behavioral patterns. PICOS criteria are presented in Table 1 . Table 1. PICOS Criteria for Inclusion of Studies Parameter Criteria Participants Infants ≤6 mo old Interventions Cow’s milk formula supplemented with prebiotics Comparisons Standard cow’s milk formula or human milk Outcomes Gut microbiome (alpha and beta diversities, taxa, and function), gut environment (gut integrity, inflammation, and metabolites, including pH, secretory immunoglobulin A, fecal calprotectin, and fecal short- and branched-chain fatty acids), infant growth (weight, weight gain, length, length gain, head circumference, weight-for-age z scores, body mass index–for-age z scores, skinfold thickness, fat mass or percent fat mass, and fat-free mass or percent fat-free mass), adverse events (safety and tolerance; eg, digestive symptoms and behavioral patterns) Study design Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Randomized controlled trial study designs were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis if they (1) were published in English or French, (2) targeted healthy infants ≤6 months of age to exclude the possibility of interaction with solid food intake, (3) intervened with cow’s milk–based, prebiotic-supplemented formula (with no additional ingredients) for ≥1 month, (4) compared the intervention with cow’s milk–based standard formula (no additional ingredients except for maltodextrin) and/or human milk, and (5) reported on the gut microbiome, gut environment, and/or growth-related measurements. Articles were excluded if those criteria were not met and for the following reasons, due to potential differences in bacterial transmission: if infants were (1) born with congenital illness or malformations that could affect the gut microbiome, growth, or body composition, (2) enrolled in the original research based on a diagnosed clinical indication for them (eg, preterm birth) or their mother (eg, hepatitis C virus infection), and (3) born to minor parent(s). Search Strategy Primary searches were performed on June 15, 2021, without minimum date limits. The search was updated in April 2024. Four electronic databases were searched: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ProQuest Dissertation & Theses, and we also searched for clinical trials registered on clinicaltrials.gov. Controlled search vocabulary (eg, “infant formula”) and keywords (eg, “obes*”) were confirmed by a health sciences research librarian. Original trials published in the English and French languages were included if they reported on any of the exposures and outcomes of interest. Search terms were adapted for each database and combined using Boolean operators to narrow the results. A sample search strategy is presented in Table 2 . Reference lists from full-text articles that met our inclusion criteria were searched to identify any additional articles of relevance. Table 2. PubMed Database Search Strategy Search no. Initial screening was conducted via review of manuscript titles and abstracts by 3 independent reviewers (M.K., K.L., and M.G.). As a preliminary step, a sample of 10% of articles was triple screened to ensure consistency among reviewers. Upon confirmation of consistency among the 3 reviewers, the remaining articles were assessed. The secondary step included full-text reviews by 2 independent reviewers (M.K. and K.L.); any discrepancies were discussed and resolved with a third independent reviewer (L.M.R.). Manuscript titles, abstracts, and full texts from the updated search were screened by 2 independent reviewers (D.C. and E.M.); any discrepancies were discussed and resolved with a third independent reviewer (M.K.). Data Extraction The data elements included were chosen through discussion among team members and were revised iteratively. Identifiers and variables included author(s), year of publication, study location, study design, study populations and characteristics (eg, mean age and/or age range, sex, birth mode), sample size, type of formula, comparator, length of exposure, follow-up duration, primary and secondary outcomes, and aim(s) of the study. The data extraction form was completed by 2 independent reviewers; any differences were resolved through discussion. Authors of trials were contacted for additional information, when necessary (eg, for standardization of statistics and units, intention-to-treat vs per-protocol values, z score calculations). Risk-of-Bias (Quality) Assessment Two independent reviewers (M.K. and K.L.) used the Cochrane Collaboration Tool (RoB 2) 23 to assess the methodological quality of the included trials. Briefly, each article was assessed across 5 domains: (1) bias arising from the randomization process, (2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (3) bias due to missing outcome data, (4) bias in measurement of the outcome, and (5) bias in selection of the reported result. Studies with “low concern” across all 5 domains were considered to have low overall assessment bias; studies with 1 or more domains with “high concern” or “some concern” were considered to have high overall assessment bias; studies with 1 some concern domain but no high concern domains were considered to have moderate overall assessment bias. Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion and arbitration by a third assessor, as required. Strategy for Data Synthesis and Analysis Findings from full-text articles were synthesized narratively using a descriptive summary, including the study problem or purpose, relevance or rationale of the study, implications for study design or methods, and possible limitations or biases. Basic descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize participant and study characteristics. A set of meta-analyses was performed. Only studies with requisite data were included in the meta-analyses. Meta-analyses using a fixed-effects model were completed if heterogeneity was not too high ( I 2 < 75%); a random-effects model was used if heterogeneity was ≥75%. Standardized mean differences (MDs) and SDs were used as summary statistics when the trials assessed the same outcome using different measurements; otherwise, raw MDs and SDs were used with 95% CIs. Per-protocol values were used if intent-to-treat values were not reported or provided by authors upon contact. Forest plots were used to display data; according to Cochrane guidelines, if the outcome of interest is adverse, the results to the left of the vertical line are set to favor the experimental over the control group, whereas if the outcome of interest is desirable, the results to the right of the vertical line are set to favor the experimental over the control group. RESULTS Study Selection and Characteristics The initial search strategy yielded 821 citations. After the removal of duplicates, 751 citations were retrieved for title and abstract screening, and 23 articles met the inclusion criteria and were reviewed in full. An additional 7 articles were reviewed that were identified from reference lists. A total of 30 eligible articles were included in the analyses. No additional articles were identified from our updated search in April 2024. Inter-rater reliability for the inclusion of full-text articles between the 2 independent reviewers was excellent (Cohen’s κ = 1.0). Of the included articles ( n = 30), more than half ( n = 16; 53.3%) reported on trials conducted in Europe, followed by the United States ( n = 9; 30%), and Asia ( n = 2; 6.7%); South America ( n = 1; 3.3%), and Africa ( n = 1; 3.3%), and 1 study was multicontinental ( n = 1; 3.3%). Herein, in-depth descriptions regarding the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus (gut composition) and growth parameters are reported, as well as brief descriptions of gut environment metrics, as well as safety and tolerance, among standard formula and human milk comparators. Please refer to the Supplementary Material online for reports on other bacteria at the phylum, family, genus, and species levels, as well as in-depth descriptions of the gut environment and safety and tolerance. Composition of the Gut Microbiota Bifidobacterium : Infant Formula Supplemented With Prebiotics vs a Standard Formula Meta-analysis Seven studies had requisite data for inclusion in the meta-analysis examining differences in Bifidobacterium between a prebiotic formula and a standard formula comparator. 24–30 The meta-analysis revealed significant differences in the abundance of Bifidobacterium between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups, favoring the prebiotic formula ( k = 7; MD: 0.49 [95% CI, 0.27-0.71]; I 2 = 13%; P < .00001) ( Figure 3 ). Figure 3. Bifidobacterium : Prebiotic Formula vs Standard Formula Meta-Analysis. df, degrees of freedom; IV, inverse variance. Fructo-oligosaccharides Seven studies used FOS as their prebiotic supplement and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 25 , 28 , 31–35 Three of these studies found significant variations in Bifidobacterium counts in infants supplemented with FOS at concentrations of 3 g L –1 , 25 4 g L –1 , 32 and 5 g L –1 . 31 They found an increased rate of change from baseline in Bifidobacterium counts at 1, 31 2, 25 and 3 months after supplementation 32 in the prebiotic formula compared with standard formula groups. In the other 4 studies, infants received FOS at concentrations ranging from 2 g L –1 to 5 g L –1 . 28 , 31 , 33 , 34 Despite similar concentrations as used in the 3 aforementioned studies, there were no significant differences in Bifidobacterium counts or abundance observed between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups at various time points, including 2-15 weeks after supplementation. 28 , 31 , 33 , 34 GOS to FOS ratios Eight studies used a 9:1 ratio of GOS to FOS (hereafter, GOS:FOS) in their prebiotic formula and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 16 , 17 , 29 , 36–40 Four of these studies used GOS:FOS concentrations of 5.2 g L –1 , 36 6 g L –1 , 16 and 8 g L –1 . 37 , 38 These studies found no significant differences in the percent increase, 37 total abundance, 36 proportion, 16 or counts 38 of Bifidobacterium between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups at measured time points. Measured time points included days 3, 37 5, 16 , 37 and 10 16 ; weeks 2-22 16 , 36–38 ; and 2 months 36 after supplementation. In contrast, the other 4 studies 36 , 38 used GOS:FOS concentrations of 4 g L –1, 29 5.2 g L –1 , 36 6 g L –1 , 39 and 8 g L –1 . 17 , 38 , 40 These studies reported significantly higher (1) Bifidobacterium counts at weeks 2 38 and 4 38 after supplementation; (2) absolute and proportions of Bifidobacterium at weeks 3, 29 6, 17 , 29 , 40 and 8 39 after supplementation; and (3) abundances at 4 months of age. 36 Galacto-oligosaccharides Three studies used GOS in their prebiotic formula and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 26 , 30 , 41 Infants supplemented with concentrations of 2.4 g L –1 GOS 30 and 4.4 g L –1 GOS 26 had significantly higher Bifidobacterium counts 3 months after supplementation 30 and at 4 months of age 26 when compared with the standard formula group. Infants fed 4 g L –1 GOS 41 had no significant differences in Bifidobacterium abundance between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups at ages 30 and 60 days. 41 OF to inulin ratios Three studies used a 50:50 ratio of OF to inulin (hereafter, OF:inulin) in their supplemented prebiotic and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 24 , 27 , 38 There were no statistically significant differences in concentrations of 4 g L –1 OF:inulin 38 and 8 g L –1 OF:inulin 27 in Bifidobacterium counts at days 14 or 28, 38 or at 3 months of the intervention period, 27 between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups. Neumer et al 24 and Veereman-Wauters et al 38 used a concentration of 8 g L –1 OF:inulin and found significantly higher Bifidobacterium counts at day 14 but not day 28 of supplementation. 38 They also found significantly higher proportions at in counts from infants of ages 2 months and 6 months, yet these differences in Bifidobacterium became nonsignificant at 12 months of age 24 in their prebiotic formula group compared with the standard formula group. Polydextrose to GOS ratios Four studies used a 1:1 ratio of 4 g L –1 polydextrose (PDX) to GOS (PDX:GOS) as their prebiotic supplement and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 42–45 Two of these studies reported no significant differences in Bifidobacterium counts at days 14 or 28 45 or at day 30 44 between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups. Although Colombo et al 42 found an increase in Bifidobacterium from baseline to day 112 in the PDX:GOS group, this increase was not significant. However, Ranucci et al 43 and Scalabrin et al 44 found significantly higher Bifidobacterium counts after a 60-day intervention period, 44 and higher Bifidobacterium levels in infants at 96 weeks of age 43 fed the prebiotic formula compared with the standard formula groups. Other prebiotics Four studies used other combinations of prebiotics and examined Bifidobacterium as an outcome. 39 , 45–47 Concentrations of 4 g L –1 PDX to GOS to lactulose (LOS) (hereafter, PDX:GOS:LOS), 45 8 g L –1 PDX:GOS:LOS, 45 6.8 g L –1 GOS:FOS (9:1) plus 1.2 g L –1 pectin-derived acidic oligosaccharides, 47 and 6 g L –1 GOS:FOS plus 2.0 g L –1 pectin-derived acidic oligosaccharides 39 were not significantly different between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups in the proportion of Bifidobacterium at days 14 and 28, 45 2 months, 39 and 26 weeks 47 after supplementation. Brück et al 46 used a prebiotic concentration of 25% α-lactalbumin (α-lac) to 15% casein glycomacropeptide (GMP) 100 mL –1 or 25% α-lac to 10% casein GMP 100 mL –1 as their prebiotic formula. There were no significant differences in Bifidobacterium counts in infants receiving either of these prebiotic concentrations showed at ages 4 or 6 months compared with the standard formula group. 46 Reports on Bifidobacterium spp Three studies examined the effects of infant formula supplemented with prebiotics on specific Bifidobacterium spp. 26 , 40 , 44 Two of these studies examined B breve concentrations; concentrations of 4.4 g L –1 GOS 26 and 6 g L –1 GOS:FOS 40 resulted in higher counts of B breve 6 weeks after supplementation 40 and at 4 months of age 26 between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups. Haarman and Knol 40 found no significant differences in the percentage of B adolescentis, B angulatum, B bifidum, B dentium, B infantis, and B longum between the group fed the prebiotic formula compared with the standard formula; however, they found a significantly lower B catenulatum population in the group fed the prebiotic formula compared with standard formula 6 weeks after supplementation. Scalabrin et al 44 used a concentration of 4 g L –1 PDX:GOS and found no significant differences in counts of B longum, B animalis , and B catenulatum at day 30 in the prebiotic formula group compared with the standard formula group; however, they found significantly higher B infantis counts at day 30 in the prebiotic formula group compared with the standard formula group. 44 At 60 days, there were significantly higher B longum counts between groups, but no significant differences in B infantis, B animalis , or B catenulatum counts. 44 Bifidobacterium : Infant Formula Supplemented With Prebiotics vs Human Milk Comparator Meta-analysis Six studies had requisite data for inclusion in the meta-analysis examining differences in Bifidobacterium counts between a prebiotic formula and a human milk comparator. 25 , 27–30 , 35 The meta-analysis revealed no significant differences in the abundance of Bifidobacterium between the 2 ( k = 6 [MD: 0.13; 95% CI, –0.09 to 0.35]; I 2 = 20%; P = .23) ( Figure 4 ). Gut Environment Results focusing on gut environment outcomes (ie, pH, sIgA, fecal calprotectin, fecal short- and branched-chain amino acids, and lactate) are presented in the Supplemental Material . In brief, prebiotic formula supplementation decreased fecal pH ( k = 3 [MD: –0.39; 95% CI, –0.57 to –0.20]; I 2 = 0%; P < .0001) compared with standard formula. No further significant differences in gut environment markers were found in meta-analyses when comparing prebiotic-supplemented formula and standard formula or human milk. Growth Parameters Twelve studies investigated the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on measures of infant growth, including weight gain 30 , 32 , 38 , 39 , 44 , 51 ; z scores for weight for age, 24 , 36 , 39 , 45 , 51 length for age, 24 , 45 , 51 weight for length, 51 and length/weight for age 36 ; head circumference 24 , 27 , 36 , 38 , 42 , 44 , 45 , 51 ; and body mass index. 24 , 32 , 38 , 42 , 44 Infant Formula Supplemented With Prebiotics vs a Standard Formula Eleven studies investigated the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on growth parameters of infants compared with standard formula. 24 , 27 , 29 , 30 , 32 , 36 , 38 , 39 , 42 , 45 , 51 Only 1 of these studies found significant differences between the prebiotic and standard formula groups. 45 Nakamura et al 45 found significantly higher weight-for-age z scores and length-for-age z scores 1 month after supplementation in infants who had formula supplemented with 4 g L –1 PDX to GOS (1:1) compared with the standard formula group. They also found that infants supplemented with 8 g L –1 PDX:GOS:LOS had significantly higher weight-for-age z scores 1 month after supplementation compared with the standard formula group. 45 The remaining trials showed no significant differences in any growth parameters between the prebiotic formula and standard formula groups at time points ranging from 2 weeks to 112 days after supplementation. 24 , 27 , 29 , 30 , 32 , 36 , 38 , 39 , 42 , 51 Infant Formula Supplemented With Prebiotics vs Human Milk Comparator Seven studies investigated the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula on growth parameters of infants compared with infants fed human milk. 27 , 29 , 30 , 36 , 38 , 44 , 45 Scalabrin et al 44 found a significantly higher mean growth rate in the prebiotic formula compared with the human milk group 2 months after supplementation. Nakamura et al 45 reported significantly higher weight-for-age and length-for-age z scores in the 4 g L –1 PDX:GOS and 8 g L –1 PDX:GOS:LOS groups compared with the human milk group 1 month after supplementation. Similarly, Closa-Monasterolo et al 27 also found significantly higher weight-for-age z scores in the 8 g L –1 OF:inulin group compared with the human milk group 3 months after supplementation. The remaining trials showed no significant differences in any growth parameters between the prebiotic formula and human milk group at time points ranging from 2 weeks to 6 months after supplementation and at ages 2, 4, 6, 9, and 12 months. 29 , 30 , 36 , 38 From our subsets of meta-analyses, no significant differences were found between groups (prebiotic formula vs standard formula or human milk) for any growth parameters (data not shown) except for weight-for-age z scores favoring the prebiotic formula group compared with the human milk group ( k = 2 [MD: 0.23; 95% CI, 0.04-0.42]; I 2 = 7%; P = .02) 27 , 45 ( Figure 7 ). Safety and Tolerance Results focusing on safety and tolerance are presented in the Supplemental Material . In brief, prebiotic-supplemented formula generally showed no significant differences in safety parameters such as adverse events, compared with standard formula groups. However, some significant findings included softer stools, higher stool frequency, and lower vomiting rates with specific prebiotic concentrations. In comparison with human milk, significant differences were noted in stool consistency and frequency for certain prebiotic concentrations, with some showing harder stools and lower stool frequency. Overall, although prebiotic supplementation had varied effects across different studies, it generally exhibited a comparable safety profile to standard formula or human milk, with some specific benefits noted in certain parameters. DISCUSSION The establishment and development of the infant gut microbiota play a crucial role in immune system maturation, nutrient metabolism, and overall health outcomes. Prebiotic supplementation in infant formula has been proposed as a strategy to mimic the benefits of HMOs in human milk, promoting the growth of beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus . In this systematic review and meta-analysis, evidence was synthesized on the effects of prebiotic-supplemented formula compared with standard formula or human milk on the composition of the gut microbiota and growth parameters in infants aged ≤6 months. These findings shed light on the variability in outcomes associated with different types and concentrations of prebiotics added to infant formula. This analysis revealed heterogeneity in the effects of prebiotic supplementation (compared with standard formula) on Bifidobacterium abundance, depending on the type and concentration of prebiotics used. Studies using GOS, FOS, GOS:FOS, OF:inulin, and PDX:GOS supplementation demonstrated inconsistent effects on Bifidobacterium counts, with some reporting significant increases whereas others showed no differences compared with standard formula. Alternatively, a recent systematic review with a similar question concluded that most studies showed an increase in fecal Bifidobacterium levels except for those supplementing with GOS, FOS, or GOS:FOS. 20 Despite conflicting narrative summaries, the meta-analysis, which included studies supplementing with a mixture of prebiotics (GOS, FOS, GOS:FOS, OF, OF:inulin), showed a positive effect, namely an increase in Bifidobacterium in the prebiotic formula compared with standard formula group. This analysis also examined the effects of prebiotic supplementation (compared with standard formula) on Lactobacillus abundance in infants. Similar to Bifidobacterium , the effects of prebiotics on Lactobacillus counts varied depending on the type and concentration of prebiotics used. Studies using FOS alone or PDX:GOS found no significant difference between the prebiotic and standard formula groups. However, studies using GOS alone or in combination with FOS reported mixed results, with some finding significant increases in Lactobacillus counts and others reporting no difference compared with standard formula groups. This heterogeneous response aligns with the findings of the Ferro et al review. 20 The meta-analysis, which included studies supplementing with a mixture of prebiotics (GOS, FOS, GOS:FOS), showed an overall null finding between groups. Comparative analysis between prebiotic-supplemented formula and human milk revealed mixed findings or no significant effect on Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus colonization. Null findings were also evident in the meta-analysis, which included similar combinations of prebiotics (GOS, FOS, GOS:FOS, OF with or without inulin). Human milk contains a myriad of bioactive components, including HMOs, which exert selective pressure on the infant gut microbiota and promote the growth of Bifidobacterium species. 52 The structural diversity of HMOs is unique to humans, with >100 different oligosaccharide structures identified in human milk, although not all structures are produced within a given mother and the types and concentrations vary between mothers. 10 In contrast, prebiotic-supplemented formula may provide a more simplified substrate profile, potentially limiting its ability to modulate microbial diversity and function to the same extent as HMOs. Therefore, it is surprising that the microbial response in the analysis was similar in the prebiotic formula and human milk groups, which may suggest that the dose and type of prebiotic used for supplementation provided a similar bifidogenic response, although other properties of human milk or HMOs (eg, pathogen anti-adhesion 53 ) could still be missing. Based on clinical outcomes, prebiotic supplementation did not demonstrate any differential effects on various growth parameters, including weight gain, length gain, and head circumference, when compared with standard formula or human milk. This conclusion is similar to that of Skórka et al, 54 who highlighted no differential effects of GOS, FOS, or GOS:FOS on growth markers between the prebiotic and standard formula groups. Indeed, despite new data, conclusions remain the same as those made by ESPGHAN’s systematic review conducted in 2011 19 ; that is, formula supplemented with prebiotics does not have adverse effects on growth. The neutral findings with human milk as a comparator are novel and may be promising because they indicate that infants who received a prebiotic formula had comparable growth outcomes to those receiving human milk. Yet, 2 studies included in the meta-analysis examined weight-for-age z scores and found significantly larger effects for the prebiotic formula compared with the human milk group. These results could imply that prebiotic-supplemented formula may be more effective in promoting weight gain than human milk, which may be relevant in the case of concerns with infant growth and weight gain. This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, due to the heterogeneity in study designs, prebiotic formulations, and microbiota analysis methods, directly comparing results across studies is challenging. Second, most included studies had relatively small sample sizes and short follow-up periods, which may affect the robustness of the results. Third, most studies did not provide details regarding sample size calculations or whether adequate power was achieved to investigate all outcomes, including growth parameters that normally require a larger sample size, compared with gut microbiome differences. Fourth, publication bias may have influenced the findings because studies reporting positive outcomes are more likely to be published. Finally, it is important to recognize that, although all formulas included in this systematic review and meta-analysis are cow's milk based, there may be notable differences in their nutritional composition that may influence infant gut microbiota and metabolic outcomes. Variability in carbohydrate sources, protein quality, fat, and iron composition among major formula brands could potentially affect the microbiota differently, leading to variations in health outcomes. Most studies included in this analysis did not provide comprehensive nutritional information beyond the presence of prebiotic supplements, limiting the ability to assess the specific impacts of these compositional differences. Future research should aim to include detailed nutritional profiles of formulas to better understand how these variations might influence infant gut microbiota and overall health outcomes. CONCLUSION This systematic review and meta-analysis provide insights into the effects of prebiotic supplementation on the infant gut microbiota composition. Among the bacterial genera found in the human gastrointestinal tract, Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus are those explored most extensively in human and animal studies. These 2 bacterial groups are recognized to have health-promoting properties, and specific strains from within them are added to commercial foods, such as infant formula, and used in probiotic supplements as a means of delivering health-associated bacteria to the host. In meta-analyses, prebiotics in infant formula showed promise in promoting the growth of Bifidobacterium compared with standard formula. However, the variability in study designs underscores the need for standardized research. Future studies should consider factors such as dose-response relationships, duration of supplementation, and other potential nutritional or bioactive additives found in human milk. documents.title: Preventive effect of probiotics on oral mucositis induced by anticancer therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oral mucositis (OM) is a prevalent and painful complication in patients undergoing anticancer treatment, which significantly impacts patients' quality of life (QoL) and adherence to therapy. The use of oral probiotics as a preventive strategy for OM has shown promise, but the clinical evidence remains inconclusive. This meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) aims to evaluate the efficacy of probiotics in preventing OM caused by radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov was conducted up to January 31, 2024, to identify eligible RCTs. The primary outcomes were the incidences of severe OM and all-grade OM. Secondary outcomes included rates of anticancer treatment completion, clinical response, requirement for enteral nutrition, time course of OM, body weight loss, QoL, and adverse events (AEs). Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.
RESULTS: A total of 12 RCTs involving 1,376 patients were included in the quantitative analysis. Probiotics administration significantly reduced the risk of severe OM (RR = 0.61, 95%CI: 0.53-0.72, P < 0.001) and all-grade OM (RR = 0.90, 95%CI: 0.82-0.98, P = 0.016) compared to the control group. Multi-strain probiotics formulations were more effective than single-strain probiotics in preventing severe OM (P = 0.011). There were no significant differences between the probiotics and control groups regarding anticancer treatment completion (RR = 1.03, 95%CI: 0.98-1.08, P = 0.198), clinical response to therapy (RR = 1.05, 95%CI: 0.94-1.17, P = 0.406), or the need for enteral nutrition (RR = 1.28, 95%CI: 0.49-3.35, P = 0.680). AEs related to probiotics were rare, with no serious AEs attributable to probiotics use.
CONCLUSIONS: Oral probiotics are both safe and effective in preventing and reducing the severity of OM in patients undergoing anticancer therapy. Multi-strain probiotics demonstrate superior efficacy compared to single-strain probiotics. Further research is warranted to confirm these findings and optimize probiotic treatment strategies for cancer patients.
documents.conclusions: Oral probiotics are both safe and effective in preventing and reducing the severity of OM in patients undergoing anticancer therapy. Multi-strain probiotics demonstrate superior efficacy compared to single-strain probiotics. Further research is warranted to confirm these findings and optimize probiotic treatment strategies for cancer patients.

Background Oral mucositis (OM) is one of the most prevalent and painful side effects experienced by cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy [ 1 ]. It affects 20–40% of patients receiving conventional chemotherapy, approximate 80% of those with hematological malignancies undergoing myeloablative conditioning prior to stem cell transplantation, and nearly all head and neck cancer patients receiving radiotherapy [ 2 , 3 ]. This unwanted and painful complication of anticancer therapy impairs essential functions, such as swallowing, chewing, and speaking, often leading to dysphagia and dysgeusia, which severely impacts patients’ ability to eat and drink [ 4 ]. OM frequently necessitates the use of enteral feeding and narcotic analgesics [ 5 ], and also increases the risk of systemic infections and hospitalizations [ 6 ]. Consequently, OM, particular in its severe form, significantly diminishes patients’ quality of life (QoL), alters nutrition status, and disrupts anticancer treatments, potentially leading to worse oncologic outcomes [ 7 ]. Notably, patients with OM face a twofold increased risk of infections and a fourfold higher risk of death compared to those without the condition [ 7 ]. Therefore, preventing and alleviating OM is essential to enhancing patient comfort, QoL, and adherence to cancer treatment. A deep understanding of OM pathogenesis could help inform effective intervention and management strategies for OM caused by radiotherapy and chemotherapy The Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer/The International Society of Oral Oncology (MASCC/ISOO) have developed clinical practice guideline recommending several interventions, including basic oral care, anti-inflammatory agents, oral cryotherapy, growth factors, cytokines, and low-level laser therapy to mitigate OM development [ 1 ]. In recent years, the role of the oral microbiome in OM pathophysiology has gained attention, with probiotics emerging as a potential preventive measure against the toxic side effects of anticancer treatments [ 8 , 9 ]. The oral cavity, second only to the gut in terms of colonization, harbors a dynamic and diverse microbiome bacterial community [ 10 ]. Researches have shown that cancer treatment can significantly alter the oral microbiota, leading to reduced microbial diversity and a shift towards pathogenic species, which suggests a connection between the oral microbiome and the development and severity of OM [ 11 – 15 ]. However, the selective elimination of oral flora, such as Candida species and Gram-negative bacilli, has not been shown to prevent severe OM in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy [ 16 ]. A promising alternative strategy focuses on maintaining a “healthy” oral microbial community through the use of probiotics. This approach promotes the growth of commensal populations that are crucial for oral epithelial health, as opposed to antimicrobial strategies targeting specific pathogens [ 4 ]. Animal models of radiotherapy- and chemotherapy-induced mucositis have demonstrated that probiotics enhance immune responses, reduce mucosal inflammation and injury, and elevate cytokine levels [ 17 – 19 ]. Several randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have also shown that probiotics administration decreases the incidence of both severe and all-grade OM compared to placebo [ 20 – 22 ]. However, other trials have not reported significant effects of probiotics on OM prevention [ 23 , 24 ]. The inconsistency in findings may be attributed to differences in sample size, anticancer treatments, probiotic strains, and control interventions across trials. To address these variations, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of available RCTs to evaluate the safety and efficacy of probiotics in preventing OM induced by anticancer therapies. Methods Literature search This systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs was conducted in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guideline (Additional file 1 ) [ 25 ]. We systematically searched electronic databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov, from inception to January 31, 2024, to identify relevant studies and registered trials. Additionally, Google Scholar was searched for grey literatures, and the first 300 items sorted by relevance were reviewed for eligibility. The following MeSH terms and their variations were used in the search: (‘probiotics’[Mesh] OR ‘probiotic*’[tiab] OR ‘synbiotic*’[tiab] OR ‘lactobacillus’[Mesh] OR ‘lactobacillus’[tiab] OR ‘lactobacilli’[tiab] OR ‘bifidobacterium’[Mesh] OR ‘bifidobacterium’[tiab]) AND (‘radiotherapy’[Mesh] OR ‘drug therapy’[Mesh] OR ‘chemoradiotherapy’[Mesh] OR ‘radiotherapy’[tiab] OR ‘chemotherapy’[tiab] OR ‘radiochemotherapy’[tiab] OR ‘chemoradiotherapy’[tiab]) AND (‘stomatitis’[Mesh] OR ‘stomatitis’[tiab] OR ‘mucositis’[tiab]) (Additional file 2 ). No language restrictions were applied. Reference lists of included studies were manually reviewed to identify additional candidates. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Study eligibility was determined using the PICOS framework. Population (P): Cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). Intervention (I): Probiotic agents or products containing probiotics. Comparison (C): Control products without probiotics or no control. Outcome (O): Incidence of severe and all-grade OM. Study design (S): RCTs. Non-randomized observational trials, animal or basic research, reviews, clinical trial protocols, or studies without control groups were excluded. Two independent researchers (B.Y., W.L.) conducted the literature search, screening, and selection. Cohen’s kappa coefficient was calculated to evaluate inter-reviewer agreement at each stage. Conflicts were resolved through discussion with a third researcher (J.S.). Outcomes and data extraction The primary outcomes were the incidences of severe OM and all-grade OM. Secondary outcomes included anticancer treatment completion rate, enteral nutrition requirement, time to OM onset, time to OM resolution or healing, OM duration, body weight loss, quality of life (QoL), and adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) attributable to study products. Two researchers (B.Y., W.L.) independently extracted data on the following: first author, publication year, cancer type, anticancer treatment, patient age and sex distribution, sample size, probiotic types, control treatments, OM diagnosis criteria, and data for the primary and secondary outcomes. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third researcher (J.S.). Methodology assessment Methodological quality was assessed independently by two researchers (B.Y. and W.L.) using the Risk of Bias (RoB) 2 tool [ 26 ]. The RoB 2 tool evaluates bias from randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and the selection of the reported data. Each domain was rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, leading to an overall judgment of bias. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third researcher (J.S.). Statistical analysis All quantitative analyses were performed using STATA 16.0 (StataCorp, TX, US). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistics and the Q-test. A fixed-effect model was applied if heterogeneity was low or moderate (I²<50% and P > 0.10 for the Q-test); otherwise, a random-effect model was used in cases of high heterogeneity. Risk ratios (RRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to estimate the preventive effect of probiotics on OM induced by anticancer treatments. Further analyses were stratified by treatment type (chemotherapy or radiotherapy only, CCRT), probiotic strains (single strain, multiple strains), and control type (placebo, non-placebo). Sensitivity analysis was conducted using the leave-one-out method to assess the robustness of pooled results by omitting one study at a time. Funnel plots and Egger’s tests were used to detect publication bias. If publication bias was suspected (Egger’s test P < 0.10), the trim-and-fill method, which imputes hypothetical unpublished negative studies, was employed to evaluate its impact on the pooled results. A P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics of trials included in meta-analysis As shown in Fig. 1 , a comprehensive literature search yielded 1,044 records. After removing duplicates, 473 unique articles remained. Upon reviewing the titles and abstracts, 434 articles were excluded, leaving 39 records for further assessment. After full-text review, 26 articles were excluded, resulting in 13 trials included for qualitative analysis. There was high levels of inter-reviewer agreement at title/abstract screening stage (kappa = 0.83) and full-text article assessment stage (kappa = 0.88). One study was excluded from the quantitative analysis because it reported OM incidence at the chemotherapy cycle level rather than at the patient level [ 27 ]. Ultimately, 12 RCTs, comprising 854 patients in the probiotics group and 522 in the control group, were included in the quantitative synthesis [ 20 – 24 , 28 – 34 ]. Patients had colorectal cancer ( n = 2), head and neck cancer ( n = 5), esophageal cancer ( n = 2), nasopharyngeal cancer ( n = 2), oral cancer ( n = 1), and central nervous system tumors ( n = 1). The anticancer treatment included chemotherapy in 5 trials, radiotherapy in 4 trials, and CCRT in 4 trials. Single-strain probiotics were used in 7 trials [ 21 , 22 , 24 , 28 , 29 , 31 , 33 ], while multi-strains probiotics were employed in 6 trials [ 20 , 23 , 27 , 30 , 32 , 34 ]. Seven studies were placebo-controlled [ 20 – 22 , 28 , 29 , 31 , 34 ]. OM was assessed using either the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria [ 21 , 29 , 30 ] or the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Severe OM was defined as grade 3 or higher OM. Baseline characteristics of all trials included in the meta-analysis are summarized in Table 1 . A pooled analysis using a fixed-effect model showed a significantly lower risk of severe OM in the probiotics group than the control group (RR = 0.61, 95%CI: 0.53–0.72, P < 0.001, Fig. 3 ). In all subgroups analyses stratified by treatment type, probiotic strain, and control type, probiotics consistently demonstrated a preventive effect on severe OM (Table 2 ). A pooled analysis using a random-effect model indicated that probiotics slightly reduced the risk of all-grade OM (RR = 0.90, 95%CI: 0.82–0.98, P = 0.016, Fig. 5 ). Subgroup analysis demonstrated a preventive effect on all-grade OM in patients undergoing chemotherapy or radiotherapy, those administered single-strain probiotics, and in placebo-controlled trials (Table 2 ). Fig. 5 Forest plot of the incidence of all-grade OM induced by anticancer therapy Secondary outcomes Anticancer treatment completion was evaluated in 10 trials [ 20 – 23 , 29 – 34 ]. A meta-analysis using a random-effect model found no significant difference of completion rates between the probiotics and control groups (RR = 1.03, 95%CI: 0.98–1.08, P = 0.198, Additional file 3 ). Four trials assessed clinical response to anticancer treatment [ 20 , 23 , 28 , 32 ], with no significant difference between the probiotics and control groups (RR = 1.05, 95%CI: 0.94–1.17, P = 0.406, Additional file 4 ). Two trials reported nutrition requirements [ 22 , 24 ], with no significant difference between the probiotics and control groups (RR = 1.28, 95%CI: 0.49–3.35, P = 0.680, Additional file 5 ). Several trials compared the time course of OM between the probiotics and control groups, including time to OM onset, time to OM resolution or healing, and OM duration. Peng et al.. also found that probiotics significantly delayed OM onset and shortened OM duration for both all-grade and severe OM [ 21 ]. Body weight loss was investigated in three trials, but the data were insufficient for meta-analysis [ 22 , 24 , 32 ]. Motoori et al.. found no significant difference in body weight loss between the probiotics and control groups (1.53 ± 1.8 vs. 1.47 ± 2.2 kg, P = 0.90) [ 32 ]. Sanctis et al.. observed a significant tendency of weight loss from baseline in both experimental and control groups but did not compare the groups directly [ 24 ]. Sharma et al.. could not calculate end-of-study weight loss due to missing data [ 22 ]. Two trials assessed QoL using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy Head and Neck (FACT-HN) questionnaire [ 22 , 24 ]. Both trials observed no significant difference in QoL between the probiotics and control groups. However, quantitative synthesis was not possible due to unavailable exact QoL scores. Adverse events related to study products Four studies included safety analyses of AEs related to study products. Two trials reported no AEs attributed to probiotics or control products [ 32 , 33 ], while the other two trials reported 2 AEs related to probiotics and 1 AE related to placebo [ 21 , 29 ]. SAEs attributable to study products were assessed in seven trials [ 20 – 22 , 24 , 28 , 29 , 33 ], but none observed any SAEs linked to probiotics or control products. Due to the rarity of these events, meta-analysis was not conducted. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis showed that omitting individual studies did not significantly affect pooled results. For instance, in the analysis of anticancer treatment completion, heterogeneity decreased from 45.6% to 0 after excluding Sharma et al. [ 22 ]. In the pooled analysis of the remaining trials with a fixed-effect model, no significant differences were observed in treatment completion rates (RR = 1.01, 95% CI: 0.98–1.05, P = 0.474, Additional file 6 ). Publication bias Egger’s test indicated potential publication bias in the analysis of severe OM ( P = 0.098). However, trim-and-fill analysis confirmed that that probiotics still significantly reduced the risk of severe OM (RR = 0.67, 95%CI 0.57–0.77, P < 0.001, Fig. 6 ). Funnel plots for all-grade OM and anticancer treatment completion were symmetrical, suggesting no obvious publication bias (Additional files 7 and 8 ). Fig. 6 Funnel plot of severe OM after trim-and-fill analysis Discussion This meta-analysis, synthesizing data from 12 RCTs involving 1,376 patients undergoing anticancer therapy, reveals a significant reduction in the incidences of both severe and all-grade OM in patients receiving probiotics. The rates of anticancer treatment completion, clinical response to therapy, and enteral nutrition requirements did not significantly differ between the probiotics and control groups. Additionally, AEs related to probiotics were rare, and no SAEs were attributed to their use. These findings suggest that probiotics are both well-tolerated and effective in preventing the development and reducing the severity of OM. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy significantly affect the oral microbiome, leading to a reduction in microbial diversity and a shift from a commensal population to a pathobiont-dominated enterotype [ 35 , 36 ]. This disruption interferes with the coordination between the oral microbiome and the host’s innate immune system, which is essential for maintaining homeostasis [ 37 ]. The abnormal colonization and altered host-microbial interaction activates the nuclear factor kappa‑B (NF-kB) signaling pathway, promoting the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and triggering an excessive immune response [ 9 , 35 ]. This, in turn, contributes to OM progression and impairs the healing capacity of the oral mucosa. Probiotics, defined as live micro-organisms that positively influence host microflora, have shown substantial health benefits in various contexts, including lowering blood pressure, improving glycemic control, and reducing levels of inflammatory biomarkers [ 38 – 40 ]. As highlighted by several clinical trials and this meta-analysis, probiotics significantly reduce the incidence of OM in patients receiving anticancer therapy. Additionally, probiotics may affect the time course of OM. For example, in head and neck cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy, Mirza et al. observed delayed OM onset and faster remission in those administered Bacillus clausii UBBC07 oral suspension compared to the placebo group [ 31 ]. Similar findings were reported in another study involving head and neck cancer patients, where Streptococcus salivarius K12 administration reduced both the duration and severity of OM [ 21 ]. The protective effects of probiotics against OM may involve several mechanisms, including modulation of immune responses, reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, maintenance of the epithelial barrier, production of antimicrobial agents, competition with pathogens, and induction of IgA secretion [ 8 ]. For instance, Lactobacillus brevis CD2 reduces inflammatory cytokines (IL-1α, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, IFN-γ) by producing arginine deiminase, which competes with nitric oxide synthase [ 41 ]. Additionally, L. brevis CD2 produces sphingomyelinase that hydrolyzes platelet-activating factor (PAF), a potent pro-inflammatory cytokine linked to radiotherapy-induced OM [ 42 ]. Lactobacillus reuteri has been shown to mitigate chemotherapy-induced mucosal damage by suppressing pro-inflammatory mediators and enhancing the expression of key antioxidant genes, such as SOD-1, GPx-1, and HO-1 [ 43 ]. Furthermore, L. reuteri produces antimicrobial compounds, inhibits pathogenic colonization, and reduces microbial translocation from the gut to tissues [ 44 ]. Streptococcus salivarius K12, known for its strong oral colonization capacity, promotes the healing of radiation-induced OM by increasing epithelial proliferation, reducing apoptosis, and enhancing mucosal thickness [ 45 ]. Several studies have examined gut-directed probiotics for OM prevention by modulating gut microbiota, with patients ingesting probiotics directly. Jiang et al. reported that CCRT disrupted intestinal microbiota diversity in the placebo group but preserved diversity in the probiotics group [ 20 ]. In another trial, esophageal cancer patients receiving probiotics ( Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus casei ) exhibited an increased number of beneficial bacteria and a reduced number of harmful bacteria in their fecal samples compared to controls [ 32 ]. A probiotic cocktail derived from bacteria screened from a cancer-free population restored intestinal microbiota structure in nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients undergoing CCRT [ 34 ]. Targeting the oral microbiota may be more directly relevant to OM prevention, given the role of the oral microbiome in its pathogenesis. For instance, Manifar et al.. used a symbiotic mouthwash in oral cancer patients, which significantly reduced OM severity in the treatment group [ 30 ]. Peng et al. demonstrated that sucking Streptococcus salivarius K12 lozenges during radiotherapy inhibited opportunistic pathogens and enriched oral commensal bacteria [ 21 , 45 ]. Thus, probiotics targeting the oral microbiome, either alone or in combination with gut-directed probiotics, may provide an effective strategy for preventing and mitigating cancer therapy-induced OM. A notable factor influencing the efficacy of probiotics in OM prevention is the selection of bacterial strains. The most commonly used strains, including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium , have proven effective in treating conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, ulcerative colitis, and acute gastroenteritis [ 46 – 49 ]. However, the bacterial strains and combinations used across the 12 RCTs in this meta-analysis varied significantly. Our quantitative synthesis of seven RCTs demonstrated that single-strain probiotics reduced the risk of severe OM by 31% (RR = 0.69, 95%CI: 0.58–0.81) [ 21 , 22 , 24 , 28 , 29 , 31 , 33 ]. In contrast, pooling data from five RCTs showed that multi-strain probiotics reduced the risk of severe OM by 63% (RR = 0.37, 95%CI: 0.24–0.58) [ 20 , 23 , 30 , 32 , 34 ]. This suggests that multi-strain probiotics may be more effective, possibly due to the synergistic effects of various strains on metabolic capacity and immune modulation [ 50 , 51 ]. There are several limitations to this study. Although our analysis included 12 trials and 1,376 cancer patients, the sample size may still be insufficient to fully assess the benefits of probiotics, especially in secondary outcomes and subgroup analyses based on anticancer therapy type, probiotics strains, and cancer type. The heterogeneity in radiation doses, chemotherapy regimens, and probiotic species, dosage, and duration among the included trials may also have influenced the observed effects. Additionally, we were unable to quantitatively assess several secondary outcomes, such as quality of life (QoL), the time course of OM, and body weight loss, due to insufficient data. Conclusion In conclusion, this meta-analysis demonstrates that probiotics are safe and may effectively reduce the incidence of both severe and all-grade OM in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. Multi-strain probiotics appear to be more effective in preventing severe OM than single-strain probiotics. These findings support the use of probiotics in managing anticancer therapy-induced OM. Future research should aim to identify more effective probiotic species and validate their clinical efficacy in preventing and treating OM in cancer patients, with the ultimate goal of providing better preventive and therapeutic options for this population. documents.title: Physicians', pharmacists', and nurses' education of patients about antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance in primary care settings: a qualitative systematic literature review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients' adherence to antibiotic treatment and related prevention of AMR is significant. Understanding healthcare professionals' strategies for advising and educating patients in primary care settings is crucial.
AIM: From the perspectives of professionals and patients, to explore how physicians, pharmacists, and nurses educate patients about antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance in primary care settings.
METHODS: A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted in MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL Complete, Eric, SocINDEX, PsycInfo, Web of Science and Scopus. The study included 102 publications, followed PRISMA recommendations and was registered in PROSPERO (reg.no. CRD4202455761). The studies were screened and selected based on specific inclusion and exclusion criteria using Covidence. Quality appraisal followed the Critical Appraisal Skills Program (CASP) qualitative study checklist. Data were extracted, and the analysis consisted of a descriptive numerical summary analysis and a qualitative thematic analysis.
RESULTS: The analyzed studies spanned multiple countries and settings and included perspectives of primary care physicians, pharmacists, nurses and patients. Two main themes emerged: (1) Relationships between professionals and patients influenced educational strategies, showing that trust and rapport between healthcare professionals and patients played a crucial role in shaping educational strategies around antibiotic use; (2) The organizational structures challenged professionals in guiding and educating patients, highlighting how limited resources, time constraints, and system-level pressures hindered healthcare professionals' ability to provide consistent and effective education. Often, structural challenges led to not educating the patients on the risks of antibiotic misuse and antimicrobial resistance. The use of delayed prescriptions emerged as a strategy for improved AMR stewardship and to meet patients' expectations for antibiotic treatment, though it raised concerns about undermining professional responsibility and authority in ensuring appropriate antibiotic use.
CONCLUSION: Healthcare professionals' role in educating patients about antibiotic use and AMR in primary care settings was complex, with different challenges faced by nurses, pharmacists and primary care physicians. These challenges extended beyond the clinical level, including relational, social and structural factors. Power dynamics, trust issues, and time pressures often hindered effective education on antibiotic use. Addressing gaps in education on antibiotic use and AMR requires acknowledging these multifaceted challenges, with future efforts focusing on better supporting healthcare professionals in this context.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD4202455761.
